Honey Bee Crisis

By: Jane Lipman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Honey bees are a critical part of our food cycle but a bacterium that causes American foulbrood disease has killed off over 50% of the bees in the Western Cape this year .The bacteria are ingested by larvae in the bee colonies and now a twenty billion industry of pollination , honey and beeswax is in danger of vanishing according to leading experts . Two thirds of the worlds crops rely on bees for fertilisation . Infected bee colonies can be treated with anti biotics but the South African bee industry is divided on this, with some worried about the dangers of the antibiotics and chemicals , and with the Chairman of the Northern Transvaal Beekeepers Jan Steenkamp saying that Cape beekeepers should "just kill all the bees in the Western Cape " .Mike Allsopp of the Agricultural Research Council disagrees says South Africa is now somewhere between a crisis and a catastrophe , and that bees are indispensable when it comes to South African food security and that a mixed approach to solving the problem MUST be used , using antibodies and working with the Department of Agriculture and developing disease resistant honey bees .So we ask what can be done to avert this crisis ? And what is being done? And why is there so much disagreement about what is the right way forward? The Department of Agriculture is only just starting to train bee inspectors unlike any other country facing this issue ...most of the big role players in the South African Bee industry will be at a conference in Pietermaritzburg this weekend , but will also be available in the Western Cape next week ...

Press Release:


Honey Bee Crisis
The Western Cape‘s honey bee populations are being decimated by American Foul Brood Disease, carelessly introduced into the country years ago and worsening year on year. We are staring down catastrophic consequences for the South African economy and our food security. The local bee industry is divided on using controversial antibiotics or burning every last infected hive. Carte Blanche asks whether it’s too late to avert a crisis and whether our government’s reaction to the problem is anywhere near adequate.


Script:


SCRIPT “BEEMAGEDDON”
Tiny honey bees are the basis of a huge global industry ,not just creating the pots of honey on our supermarket shelves , they are the key to the pollination of commercial farm crops and fruit trees across the planet .One out of every three or four bites of food we all eat is bee pollinated .But bees are being killed at an alarming rate and our food supplies are threatened . Bees are affected by the changing environment and now in Japan and China some crops are pollinated by hand .
60 per cent of South Africa’s pollinated crops are in the Western Cape.

STANDUP Claire Mawisa A twelve billion rand agricultural industry in the Western Cape which relies heavily on bee pollination is under threat from American Foul Brood disease . Bee keepers are divided on how to deal with this ticking time bomb .

Sound up Brendan Ashley Cooper “Without bees our fruit farmers will not be able to survive “

Brendan Ashley Cooper is a third generation Beekeeper in the Western Cape who has been encouraging beekeepers to join their local association .

Sound up Brendan Ashley Cooper
We first identified AFB in the Western Cape in 2009, the worst was expected, it did not happen. What I think has happened is that the spore levels have taken time to reach a stage where we actually see visible symptoms within side the hives , and that has just been a longer period than we expected and suddenly the spore levels are high within the bee hives and we are suddenly seeing a lot more AFB as the spore levels have risen

American Foulbrood is an ancient world wide bacterium that is deadly for honey bees , but has only been in Sub Saharan Africa for the last six years . Honey was brought into South Africa through a SADEC country, but in an oversight no one checked its origins . It was from China . This honey went into Cape Town and the bees became infected .

SECTION ON IMPORTED HONEY AND IRRADIATION HERE
In fact we are importing up to 3000 tons of honey per year from China , as we don’t have a shortage in South Africa. That honey goes to centres in South Africa to be irradiated, where it is monitored by the Department of Health . The irradiation destroys all the living bacteria and organisms . The honey then doesn't have nutritional content, but is said not to be harmful to humans. Labels have to say the honey was irradiated .With American Foulbrood Disease on the increase we may have to import even more honey .
Mike Allsopp explained exactly what the disease is.

Sound Up Mike Allsopp shows Claire
“the diagnostic features that you re looking for , you are looking for cells that are darkened , sometimes they are a little bit darker and they have collapsed.
And often they have holes in them , perforations in them , and
Worker bees pick up AFB spores from infected honey with their mouth parts and then they return to the hive . The infected food is deposited and the nurse bees feed the baby larvae brood food , the larvae get infected and the spores of AFB grow in their guts.The larvae die, and billions of spores are released, infecting the colony .
If we were to open up some of those ,then the larvae has collapsed and it forms this gooey brown mess and this drawn out stringy mess , that is completely diagnostic.

There is no other brood disease that does that …it has sporulated inside the larvae and has produced literally on average for one cell , about three trillion spores .

Mike Allsopp sound up
Within that wider Cape Town area , in the last eighteen months , every commercial beekeeping operation that we have looked at , every single one has got AFB .
MAP HERE
The disease has moved from the farms around Cape Town AND OUDTSHOORN ….AND IT HAS SPREAD , VIA BEEKEEPERS MOVING THEIR HIVES ,TO ALMOST THE WHOLE OF THE WESTERN CAPE .
Sound up Mike Allsopp
We need to treat the Western Cape as a separate country in terms of honey, and we have to not move honey from the Western Cape to other parts of South Africa and in particular to other parts of Africa .

Paul Ransom , one of the 60 Bee keepers in the country, has looked after bees since the age of 12 .AFB has almost destroyed his business.

Sound up Paul
When Brendan got AFB in 2009 , I inspected my hives and I found seventeen hives with the disease and there was a lot of speculation that the bees would be able to handle it. I did very little in removing the bees that were infected. It spread through my business like wildfire and in the last four months I have lost 350 hives .
Claire question: What does that mean for your business?
Paul
Well , half my hives are gone and I have to rebuild again so it's huge huge cost to me to rebuild what has now been destroyed.
Paul Ransom supplies bee hives for fruit pollination to apple farm managers like Johan Van As in Grabouw .Johan says that the AFB that came in from the imported honey is going to have a big impact soon .

Johan Van As answer “As soon as next year , as the coming picking season we can feel the effect. I certainly hope that it's not going to happen but we can't foresee ….It's going to happen within the next seven months …

STATS
Johan Van As supplies 14 % of South Africa’s apples. He would use two pollination colonies of about 60,000 bees per hectare of apple trees .Its double the amount of bees for pears and quadruple that for plums . Some big growers take up to 2000 hives for their entire operation from the end of August till first week of October per year.

If bees can't be used for pollination what are alternatives ?

Well there's no substitute for bees to do pollination - not even from the chemical side ..

CLAIRE STAND UP LINK HERE
Claire says , whats the responsible way to remove or destroy ?

The ultimate control method is if you have highly skilled and compliant bee keepers and regulatory authorities that actually enforce the regulations then you can reduce the levels of infection within the wider bee population by burning and eliminating all the infected colonies .
If you do not have those levels of compliance , or a country that doesn't want to follow that type of route , the only other route that is followed around the world is just to use antibiotics.

Even though the Department of Agriculture allows importers to bring in honey treated with antibiotics , it is illegal to use antibiotics such as Oxy Tetra Cyclin on bees at the moment .
But this is what we are going to have to do , we are going to have to use OTC, every hive that goes to pollination to try and subdue and suppress this thing from spreading even further.

Mike McIntyre is an outspoken honey bee farmer in Durbanville .
All pollinators who register with government , and when they register by implication they say that they are going to use antibiotics and every hive that goes to pollination must be dosed with teramycin, or whatever the government recommends .

Like many, Brendan Ashley Cooper is ambivalent,and doesn't believe antibiotics are the solution …
The AFB bacterium over time becomes resistant to it , with continual applications of antibiotics , which is what one has to do when using antibiotics. There's no stopping because, as you stop using antibiotics, three or four months later the spores which were sitting in the hive - which are incredibly tough - start to germinate. They are fed to the larvae and the larvae become infected and there you have the problem again ….

Mike Allsopp

Already in America and Argentina we have resistance to the anti biotics and then you get onto this treadmill , you have to go from one antibiotic to the next antibiotic , it is a short term interim measure it dosent deliver a long term solution .The only long term solution is the bees must either manage it themselves , or the bees must manage it themselves with a really active bee keeping fraternity that are helping them along .
Mike Mcintyre
There are beekeepers that are already using anti biotics illegally , its not a secret ,
Claire How do you administer the antibiotics to the bees?
They put the powder in the notches of the frames and the bees run through it and nurse bees ingest it and then they feed the larvae with this, teramycin or whatever is being used, and that kills the infection

Riaan Van Zyl is the sole National Co-ordinator of Bee Diseases for DAFF.

Claire: What can beekeepers do to assist with the problem ?
The bee keepers can do a lot. There's not much DAFF can do - DAFF on its own , it's not possible for DAFF to control the disease. Beekeepers have to be vigilant; they have to look out in their colonies for AFB, if they detect the disease to deal with it immediately.

Paul
There are probably a thousand bee keepers in the Western Cape, of which only 65 belong to the Association, so there is a very low compliance.


Mike Allsopp
The management of the disease is only as good as its weakest links. If you’ve got an operation in the middle of a city that refuses to comply, all the other beekeepers in the vicinity - even if they are being as compliant as possible and they are being as vigilant as possible - that one bee keeper who is refusing to comply will infect everyone else.

Other beekeeping countries around the world have found different solutions to the problem.
New Zealand is the prime example of how to tackle AFB. When you get of AFB you just burn it , OK, but they had government support. We can't afford to actually burn hives .
You can't afford to burn it but they had government support .

100 million bees have died from AFB in the Western Cape, and when Spring comes there might not be enough for pollination. Countrywide the industry is worth R20 billion , and it's facing possible ruin. And if the disease spreads north, the impact is big .
If AFB were to spread through the rest of Africa it could have substantial conservation and human implications in Africa .

PROMOS
The majority of honey bees in the Western Cape have been infected by an exotic disease. Is government doing enough to protect this agricultural industry? TEN SECONDS
The honey bee plays a crucial part in a twelve billion rand industry; it doesn't exist just to create honey for our consumption, and it is under threat TEN SECONDS
American Foulbrood Disease or AFB is in the Western Cape. AFB has spread and has reached a critical point. We have unregistered beekeepers , not enough inspectors, and even if we did have inspectors ,they cannot enforce legislation FIFTEEN SECONDS
The majority of honey bees in the Western Cape have been infected by an exotic disease. Is government doing enough to protect this agricultural industry ? “ Without bees our fruit farmers will not be able to survive. FIFTEEN SECONDS

Paul Ransom supplies bee hives for fruit pollination to apple farm managers like Johan Van As in Grabouw .Johan says that the AFB that came in from the imported honey is going to have a big impact soon . Johan Van As answer “As soon as next year , as the coming picking season we can feel the effect. I certainly hope that it's not going to happen but we can't foresee ….It's going to happen within the next seven months … STATS Johan Van As supplies 14 % of South Africa’s apples. He would use two pollination colonies of about 60,000 bees per hectare of apple trees .Its double the amount of bees for pears and quadruple that for plums . Some big growers take up to 2000 hives for their entire operation from the end of August till first week of October per year. If bees can't be used for pollination what are alternatives ? Well there's no substitute for bees to do pollination - not even from the chemical side .. CLAIRE STAND UP LINK HERE Claire says , whats the responsible way to remove or destroy ? The ultimate control method is if you have highly skilled and compliant bee keepers and regulatory authorities that actually enforce the regulations then you can reduce the levels of infection within the wider bee population by burning and eliminating all the infected colonies . If you do not have those levels of compliance , or a country that doesn't want to follow that type of route , the only other route that is followed around the world is just to use antibiotics. Even though the Department of Agriculture allows importers to bring in honey treated with antibiotics , it is illegal to use antibiotics such as Oxy Tetra Cyclin on bees at the moment . But this is what we are going to have to do , we are going to have to use OTC, every hive that goes to pollination to try and subdue and suppress this thing from spreading even further. Mike McIntyre is an outspoken honey bee farmer in Durbanville . All pollinators who register with government , and when they register by implication they say that they are going to use antibiotics and every hive that goes to pollination must be dosed with teramycin, or whatever the government recommends . Like many, Brendan Ashley Cooper is ambivalent,and doesn't believe antibiotics are the solution … The AFB bacterium over time becomes resistant to it , with continual applications of antibiotics , which is what one has to do when using antibiotics. There's no stopping because, as you stop using antibiotics, three or four months later the spores which were sitting in the hive - which are incredibly tough - start to germinate. They are fed to the larvae and the larvae become infected and there you have the problem again …. Mike Allsopp Already in America and Argentina we have resistance to the anti biotics and then you get onto this treadmill , you have to go from one antibiotic to the next antibiotic , it is a short term interim measure it dosent deliver a long term solution .The only long term solution is the bees must either manage it themselves , or the bees must manage it themselves with a really active bee keeping fraternity that are helping them along . Mike Mcintyre There are beekeepers that are already using anti biotics illegally , its not a secret , Claire How do you administer the antibiotics to the bees? They put the powder in the notches of the frames and the bees run through it and nurse bees ingest it and then they feed the larvae with this, teramycin or whatever is being used, and that kills the infection Riaan Van Zyl is the sole National Co-ordinator of Bee Diseases for DAFF. Claire: What can beekeepers do to assist with the problem ? The bee keepers can do a lot. There's not much DAFF can do - DAFF on its own , it's not possible for DAFF to control the disease. Beekeepers have to be vigilant; they have to look out in their colonies for AFB, if they detect the disease to deal with it immediately. Paul There are probably a thousand bee keepers in the Western Cape, of which only 65 belong to the Association, so there is a very low compliance. Mike Allsopp The management of the disease is only as good as its weakest links. If you’ve got an operation in the middle of a city that refuses to comply, all the other beekeepers in the vicinity - even if they are being as compliant as possible and they are being as vigilant as possible - that one bee keeper who is refusing to comply will infect everyone else. Other beekeeping countries around the world have found different solutions to the problem. New Zealand is the prime example of how to tackle AFB. When you get of AFB you just burn it , OK, but they had government support. We can't afford to actually burn hives . You can't afford to burn it but they had government support . 100 million bees have died from AFB in the Western Cape, and when Spring comes there might not be enough for pollination. Countrywide the industry is worth R20 billion , and it's facing possible ruin. And if the disease spreads north, the impact is big . If AFB were to spread through the rest of Africa it could have substantial conservation and human implications in Africa . PROMOS The majority of honey bees in the Western Cape have been infected by an exotic disease. Is government doing enough to protect this agricultural industry? TEN SECONDS The honey bee plays a crucial part in a twelve billion rand industry; it doesn't exist just to create honey for our consumption, and it is under threat TEN SECONDS American Foulbrood Disease or AFB is in the Western Cape. AFB has spread and has reached a critical point. We have unregistered beekeepers , not enough inspectors, and even if we did have inspectors ,they cannot enforce legislation FIFTEEN SECONDS The majority of honey bees in the Western Cape have been infected by an exotic disease. Is government doing enough to protect this agricultural industry ? “ Without bees our fruit farmers will not be able to survive. FIFTEEN SECONDS

metadata.Summary: Honey bees are a critical part of our food cycle but a bacterium that causes American foulbrood disease has killed off over 50% of the bees in the Western Cape this year .The bacteria are ingested by larvae in the bee colonies and now a twenty billion industry of pollination , honey and beeswax is in danger of vanishing according to leading experts . Two thirds of the worlds crops rely on bees for fertilisation . Infected bee colonies can be treated with anti biotics but the South African bee industry is divided on this, with some worried about the dangers of the antibiotics and chemicals , and with the Chairman of the Northern Transvaal Beekeepers Jan Steenkamp saying that Cape beekeepers should "just kill all the bees in the Western Cape " .Mike Allsopp of the Agricultural Research Council disagrees says South Africa is now somewhere between a crisis and a catastrophe , and that bees are indispensable when it comes to South African food security and that a mixed approach to solving the problem MUST be used , using antibodies and working with the Department of Agriculture and developing disease resistant honey bees .So we ask what can be done to avert this crisis ? And what is being done? And why is there so much disagreement about what is the right way forward? The Department of Agriculture is only just starting to train bee inspectors unlike any other country facing this issue ...most of the big role players in the South African Bee industry will be at a conference in Pietermaritzburg this weekend , but will also be available in the Western Cape next week ...
